analysis.one_liner: Strips federal regulators of any say over fracking on federal land, leaving it entirely to the states.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a Senate hearing or vote, so federal authority over fracking on federal land remained in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have taken away the federal government's power to regulate hydraulic fracturing ("fracking") on federal land — national forests, public lands, and other federal property — and handed that power entirely to the states where the drilling happens. At the time, the Obama administration's Interior Department was writing the first federal rules for fracking on federal land, including requirements to disclose chemicals used and to test wells; this bill would have blocked those rules from applying, leaving each state to set its own standards with no national floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land, which would have faced only state rules instead of the pending federal standards requiring public disclosure of fracking chemicals and federal well-integrity requirements. States' oil and gas regulators would also have gained final say.

how_it_helps.text: It would have given states exclusive authority over fracking on all land within their borders, including federal land, preempting any federal regulation of the drilling process itself.

The bill's findings argue state regulation is adequate, citing state and industry-funded studies, and cite federal officials who said they had not seen proven cases of fracking contaminating groundwater.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near federal land where drilling occurs, who would have depended on whichever state's rules happened to apply, with no national standard on chemical disclosure or well testing. All taxpayers share ownership of the federal land being fracked.

drawbacks.text: It would have stripped the Interior Department of authority to set nationwide fracking standards on federal land, leaving each state to decide — a patchwork where some states might require full chemical disclosure and baseline water testing and others might require little.

The Obama administration's pending BLM rule also would have required disclosure of fracking chemicals; under this bill, residents near federal drilling sites could not count on learning what chemicals were pumped underground, and the public land their taxes own would be drilled under the weakest state rule among the choices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered oil and gas companies a single, cheaper set of state rules and blocked a federal fracking rule before it could be finalized. That benefit came entirely at the expense of the one uniform national standard for drilling chemicals on federal land — the standard that protects residents near those wells. The bill died without a vote, so the regulatory landscape was unchanged, but an honest reader should note the debate was genuinely two-sided: states have long experience regulating oil and gas, while federal regulators argued federal land is a national asset needing uniform rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Inhofe of Oklahoma introduced the bill on June 26, 2013, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the same day.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or a House companion vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
All 18 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats signed on.
The bill would have overridden the Obama administration's pending plan, announced in 2011, to issue federal rules governing fracking on federal land administered by the Bureau of Land Management.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Bureau of Land Management kept its authority to write national fracking rules for federal land, and the oil and gas industry avoided a federal preemption benefiting it without ever having to win a vote. Residents near federal drilling sites kept the prospect of a single national standard.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal regulators kept fracking authority; industry avoided a vote

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give states sole regulatory authority over fracking, including on federal land.

for.name: 18 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors including Vitter, Portman, Cruz, Paul, and Cornyn

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were Republicans and the bill died in committee without any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have blocked pending federal fracking rules on federal land, sparing drillers a federal permit, chemical-disclosure, and well-integrity regime in favor of state rules, which are typically less costly. It was written and sponsored by senators from major oil- and gas-producing states.
The bill would have removed the agency's authority to regulate fracking on the federal land it manages, nullifying its 2011–2013 rulemaking effort.
